source.title_on_document: Large Language Models Improve Hypothesis Generation by Reducing Effort

supplement.where: SI Appendix, cited throughout but not attached; OSF holds preregistrations, surveys, raw data and R code: https://osf.io/pdjwh/?view_only=d4d76b6c6e9343e99bcc146a68fbd578 (p. 11-12)
supplement.holds: Table S1 (data-collection dates, betting odds), Table S2 (preregistered N, dropout rates, final sample sizes), Table S3 (knowledge screen), Table S4 (exclusions of no-LLM participants who used an LLM), Table S5 (accuracy, confidence, calibration statistics), Section 3 (accuracy/confidence/calibration details), Section 4 (robustness: no exclusions, gender covariate, standings benchmark), Tables S12-S16 (percentile benchmarks, quartiles), Table S21 (crowd-level unique teams), Section 5 (ancillary occupation-guessing experiment). Per-arm Ns for every experiment and all statistics for the crowd-level homogeneity analysis sit only there.

paper_design_summary: Four preregistered online experiments (Prolific and MTurk, N = 396, 213, 803, 400) randomly assigned participants to use an LLM (Perplexity AI or Google Bard) or to use their own judgment plus an optional web browser or search engine while listing which MLB or NFL teams would make that season's playoffs. Experiment 3 crossed LLM use with a 10-cent-per-correct-team incentive, and Experiment 4 crossed LLM use in a first and a second listing stage. The scored outputs are the number of teams listed (hypotheses), the number and percent of accurate teams (benchmarked against betting odds), plus self-reported confidence and calibration; a crowd-level count of unique teams is reported only in the SI.

eligibility.reason: Criteria 1 and 2 are met in Experiments 1-4: individuals were randomized by Qualtrics to an LLM (Perplexity or Bard) or to own judgment plus optional search, with 213 to 803 people analyzed per experiment (p. 11-13). The doubt is scope and criterion 3. The task is forecasting which MLB/NFL teams make the playoffs, a closed set with correct answers benchmarked to betting odds (p. 4), not an output judged on novelty, originality, usefulness, or creativity as the codebook's definition of a creative or ideation task requires. The primary outcome is a count of teams listed, which matches the codebook's 'fluency' construct in form, and the paper reports a crowd-level unique-team count as a homogeneity check (p. 11), but that check has no statistics in this PDF (SI Table S21). My lean is exclusion (outside the creativity scope); flagged for Review 1.

one_line_finding: In four online RCTs, participants randomly assigned to an LLM listed more playoff teams than those using their own judgment plus search (Exp 1: 8.72 vs 5.99, d = 0.745; Exp 2: 8.43 vs 5.42, d = 0.676; Exp 4 pooled: 7.50 vs 6.07, d = 0.356; pp. 5-7), with similar percent accuracy, and a 10-cent incentive closed the gap in Exp 3 (9.87 vs 9.22, p = .306; p. 6).
open_questions: Is listing which sports teams will make the playoffs (a forecasting task with a closed set of correct answers) inside the creativity section's scope, and does a count of listed hypotheses qualify as 'fluency' under criterion 3?
Comparison type: the no-LLM control was told it could use a search engine but was not required to; coded ai_vs_active, though ai_vs_bau is arguable.
Per-arm Ns, randomized counts, dropout, and the number of no-LLM participants excluded for using an LLM are only in SI Tables S2 and S4, which are not in this PDF.
The crowd-level homogeneity (unique teams) result is reported only in SI Table S21; the SI is needed to extract any diversity statistic.
Abstract total N = 1,814, but the four experiments sum to 396 + 213 + 803 + 400 = 1,812 (p. 2 vs pp. 12-13).
Reported percentage gains differ across the document: 36% on average (abstract, p. 2), 18% to 55% (significance statement, p. 2), 30% to 58% (summary of findings, p. 4).
Fig. 3 legend mentions ** p < 0.01, but the figure shows only * markers (p. 8).
notes: Self-reported confidence (percent of listed teams the participant expects to be correct) and calibration (confidence minus accuracy) are not listed as outcomes because they rest on self-report; the paper reports LLM users were less confident and underconfident (p. 8, Fig. 4c-d, SI Table S5). Experiment 2 also asked for a single most-likely team (final prediction), not analyzed in the main text. Robustness checks (no exclusions, search users vs non-users, gender covariate, standings benchmark, quartiles, percentile benchmarks) are in SI Sections 4 and Tables S12-S16. PDF page numbers used as locators (title page = p. 1).
